decisions.reason: With type resolved as replication and the target original resolved as Howitz et al. (2003, Nature, ref. 6, DOI 10.1038/nature01960), the blind coder's 'statistically successful but flawed' verdict is correct over 'failed'. Addressing the parent scope objection: the original SIRT1 activation assay in Howitz et al. (2003) used the fluorescently labeled Fluor de Lys-SIRT1 peptide substrate (whereas native PGC-1a deacetylation had not previously been tested, p. 620). When the authors re-tested resveratrol using the original Fluor de Lys-SIRT1 substrate, they obtained the original dose-dependent activation (Figure 1C), but their central thesis is that this original assay is an experimental artifact because the peptide functions as a SIRT1 substrate solely due to the covalent fluorophore (Figure 1A) and resveratrol fails to activate SIRT1 with valid substrates lacking the fluorophore (unlabeled p53 peptide in Figure 1C, purified PGC-1a in Figure 2, and cellular PGC-1a in Figure 3). This directly matches the codebook rule for 'statistically successful but flawed' ('we replicated the effect using the original materials, but show that they are not a valid test of the claim' as the paper's main message).
